title: Same subnet or different subnet?
summary: Every packet starts with one decision: local or remote. This lesson traces that decision end to end and shows the two very different failure signatures it produces.

sections.heading: Two paths out of the host
sections.html:
Once the kernel knows the destination IP, it consults the routing table. There are really only two outcomes that matter for a directly attached host:

On-linkThe destination matches a proto kernel scope link route. The host needs the destination's own link-layer address, so it sends an ARP request (IPv4) or an NDP neighbour solicitation (IPv6) for the destination IP.
Off-linkThe destination matches a route with a via next hop, usually the default gateway. The host needs the gateway's link-layer address. The destination IP inside the packet never changes.

Notice what does not change: the destination IP. A frame is rewritten at every hop, but the IP packet survives end to end (ignoring NAT). Interviewers use this to separate people who understand encapsulation from people who repeat 'the router changes the IP'.

sections.heading: A concrete trace
sections.html:
Host 10.20.30.44/24, gateway 10.20.30.1, destination 10.20.31.7:

# 1. routing lookup10.20.31.7 -> not in 10.20.30.0/24 -> matches default 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.20.30.1# 2. neighbour resolution for the NEXT HOPARP: who-has 10.20.30.1 tell 10.20.30.44       -> 10.20.30.1 is-at 52:54:00:aa:bb:01# 3. frame on the wiresrc MAC = host NIC      dst MAC = 52:54:00:aa:bb:01src IP  = 10.20.30.44    dst IP  = 10.20.31.7      TTL 64

The same host reaching 10.20.30.99 instead:

10.20.30.99 -> inside 10.20.30.0/24 -> on-linkARP: who-has 10.20.30.99 tell 10.20.30.44      -> 10.20.30.99 is-at 52:54:00:cc:dd:02src MAC = host NIC      dst MAC = 52:54:00:cc:dd:02src IP  = 10.20.30.44    dst IP  = 10.20.30.99

sections.heading: The two failure signatures
sections.html:
Broken thingSymptomEvidence on Linux
Mask too wideSome remote destinations fail, others work; the gateway itself pings fineip route shows an unexpectedly large on-link prefix; ip neigh shows FAILED/INCOMPLETE for offline addresses
Gateway wrong / unreachableEverything off-link fails, everything on-link worksip neigh cannot resolve the gateway; ip route get 8.8.8.8 points at the wrong next hop
Gateway itself downAll off-link fails, including the gateway's own IPARP for gateway fails; ping to gateway fails
Local link downNothing works, not even on-linkip link shows NO-CARRIER/DOWN; ip addr has no address

Learn these four signatures and a large fraction of case studies in this application become quick to read. Notice that none of them are DNS problems, even though users will describe them as 'the internet is down'.

sections.heading: Where ARP fits in IP addressing
sections.html:
ARP is not a separate concern bolted on later; it is the bridge between the IP addressing plan and the Ethernet segment. Its scope is always the local broadcast domain, which is exactly why the mask matters. Three properties worth stating explicitly in an interview:

  • ARP resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC on the same link, nothing more.
  • ARP requests are broadcast, replies are unicast, and results are cached in the neighbour table for a while (base_reachable_time).
  • A host may answer ARP for any address it owns on that interface, and Linux defaults favour the weak host model — that is why ARP-based troubleshooting surprises people.

checks.prompt: A host with 172.16.4.10/22 sends a packet to 172.16.7.20. What happens?
options: The switch routes it because both hosts are on the same VLAN
The host cannot decide and sends to both
It is off-link, so the packet goes to the default gateway
It is on-link, so the host ARPs for 172.16.7.20 directly
checks.explanation: /22 covers 172.16.4.0 - 172.16.7.255. 172.16.7.20 is inside that range, so it is on-link and the host resolves 172.16.7.20's MAC directly.

why_wrong.2: You treated /22 as /24. With a /22 the address space spans four /24 blocks.
why_wrong.1: There is no ambiguous case — the AND comparison is exact.
why_wrong.0: Layer 2 switches do not route, and 'same VLAN' is not the same test as 'same subnet' (though they usually match).

checks.prompt: Which command shows exactly which next hop the kernel will use for a destination, without sending traffic?
checks.explanation: ip route get performs the lookup the kernel would perform and prints the chosen route, source address and interface. It sends nothing.

why_wrong.2: ping -R records routes in the IP header, but it still sends packets and often does not work.
why_wrong.3: traceroute sends probe packets toward the destination.
why_wrong.1: ss shows sockets, not route selection.

connect.title: ARP / NDP
connect.text: The gateway decision produces an ARP request. A failed gateway decision looks like an ARP problem.

connect.title: Routing
connect.text: The 'same subnet' test and the routing table are the same machinery: connected routes are generated from the interface prefixes.

connect.title: Troubleshooting
connect.text: ip route + ip neigh answer 'is the problem local or upstream?' before you touch ping or DNS.

interview.q: A host can reach its own subnet but nothing else. What are your first three commands and why?
interview.a: ip link (is the interface up with carrier), ip addr (is the address and mask sensible), ip route (is there a default route and is it plausible). Then ip neigh / ping the gateway to separate 'no route' from 'gateway unreachable'.

interview.q: Why can a host with a correct IP and correct gateway still fail to reach the internet?
interview.a: Because the mask is part of the configuration. A wrong mask makes the host treat remote destinations as on-link, so it ARPs instead of routing. Also possible: missing NAT, firewall, upstream routing, or a gateway that has no path onward.
